In SQL Server, SUM(Amount) {{c1::OVER}} (PARTITION BY CustomerID) calculates a total alongside each customer's rows.
column2:
OVER makes the aggregate keep individual rows instead of collapsing them into groups.
Review source

column1: To total Amount separately per customer, use SUM(Amount) OVER ({{c1::PARTITION BY CustomerID}}).
column2:
The same customer's total can repeat on each of that customer's orders. Other customers' amounts are excluded from that calculation.
Review source

column1: With unique ProductID, ROW_NUMBER() OVER ({{c1::ORDER BY Price DESC, ProductID}}) numbers highest prices first and breaks ties by ProductID.
column2:
The price sets the main ordering and ProductID resolves ties. This window order does not sort the returned result by itself.
Review source

column1: For SQL Server SUM with window ORDER BY but no explicit frame, the default is {{c1::RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW}}.
column2:
RANGE extends the frame through peers tied on the sort keys. Use ROWS when you want the frame to end at the current position.
Review source

column1: To divide products into four roughly equal-sized price groups, use {{c1::NTILE(4)}} OVER (ORDER BY Price DESC).
column2:
NTILE divides by row positions, not distinct price values. A tie can therefore fall on both sides of a group boundary.
Review source

column1: With unique OrderID, a row-by-row running total uses SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID {{c1::ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW}}).
column2:
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING starts at the first row in the partition. CURRENT ROW ends at the current row's position.
Review source

column1: With unique OrderID, AVG(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID ROWS BETWEEN {{c1::2 PRECEDING}} AND CURRENT ROW) averages up to three orders.
column2:
The frame uses the available positions at the start. The second row can average only two values.
Review source

column1: A frame covering the current row and up to two following rows uses ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND {{c1::2 FOLLOWING}}.
column2:
The frame stops early if it reaches the end of the partition. It does not pull rows from the next partition.
Review source

column1: When omitted, the row offset for LAG and LEAD defaults to {{c1::1}}.
column2:
LAG reads backward and LEAD reads forward by that number. The window ordering defines the previous and next positions.
Review source

column1: On a partition's first row, LAG(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) returns {{c1::NULL}}.
column2:
No prior row exists in this partition. An explicitly supplied default would let you choose a different value.
Review source

column1: With unique OrderID, change from the previous amount uses Amount - {{c1::LAG(Amount,1,0)}} OVER (ORDER BY OrderID).
column2:
When a previous row exists, its amount is subtracted. Zero applies only when that requested row is absent.
Review source

column1: To read Amount two rows ahead, use LEAD(Amount,{{c1::2}},0) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID).
column2:
The offset counts ahead in window order. Near the partition end, zero supplies the value for a missing second following row.
Review source

column1: With unique OrderID and default NULL handling, {{c1::FIRST_VALUE(Amount)}} OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) returns the first ordered Amount.
column2:
The first ordered row supplies the value even if its Amount is NULL. It is not necessarily the smallest Amount.
Review source

column1: With unique OrderID, LAST_VALUE(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID {{c1::ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING}}) reaches the partition's final row.
column2:
The upper frame boundary reaches the final ordered row for every result row. The default frame can stop much earlier.
Review source

column1: The first row of any SQL Server PERCENT_RANK partition has a result of {{c1::0}}.
column2:
The first rank contributes zero in the relative-rank calculation. Ties at that rank receive the same result.
Review source

column1: For one partition containing ascending values 10,20,20, CUME_DIST() gives both 20 rows {{c1::1.0}}.
column2:
For each 20, the count includes the other 20 as a peer. Both divide three qualifying values by three total values.
Review source

column1: SQL Server ranking functions reject {{c1::ROWS and RANGE}} frame clauses.
column2:
An aggregate can define a frame, but a ranking function uses the ordered partition without one.
Review source

column1: In LAG(Amount,1,0), the final argument supplies {{c1::the value for a missing preceding row}}.
column2:
If the preceding row exists and its Amount is NULL, LAG returns that NULL under default NULL handling.
Review source
